It’s mostly at night, or when I’m driving in to work before the sun even comes up. I just sit there and keep thinking that my family—my wife, the kids, even though they're older now—that they might actually just be better off if I didn't wake up in the morning. I realized how real it was starting to feel. So I went inside and I actually told my supervisor about it. I've known the guy for twenty years, and I just broke down and said, "I'm having these thoughts about not waking up." Well, doc... that’s the thing, I just... I don't know what happened to me. I used to be a guy who always had something going on, always had a project or something to look forward to. But lately... I don't know. I walk past the garden and the weeds are taking over, and I just look at it. I look at the tomatoes rotting on the vine, and I don't even care. I walk into the garage and see my workbench, and it just... it feels like it belongs to somebody else. Like some other guy used to stand there and sand wood. I don't want to talk to anybody. I don't want to stand around. I just want to go home and sit in the quiet. It’s like all the color just got washed out of everything I used to like doing.

Well, doc... that’s... that’s the real reason I’m sitting in this chair right now. Because, see, it started out as just this heavy feeling, like I said, just feeling like everything was gray and empty after my girl left. But then... then it started getting darker. 

I’d be lying in bed at night, staring up at the ceiling fan going round and round, and my wife would be asleep next to me, and I’d just think... "What if I just didn't wake up?" And at first, it was just a passing thought, you know? Like, "Man, it would be so much easier to just sleep through all this." But then it started sticking. It started playing on a loop in my head. I'd be driving to work, looking at the road, and the thought would just pop up: "They'd probably be better off. My wife wouldn't have to deal with me moping around like a ghost. My daughter’s off starting her life, she doesn't need a dad who can't even get out of his recliner." 

It got to the point where it wasn't just a thought anymore, it felt like... like this awful, heavy truth that I couldn't shake. And it scared me. It really scared me, doc. I’ve always been the provider, the guy who takes care of things, and suddenly my own brain is telling me the best way to take care of them is to just... not be here. 

I didn't tell my wife. I couldn't. But I was at work, sitting in my office at the plant, and I just... I broke down. I don't cry. I'm a 57-year-old manager, I don't sit at my desk and cry. But I did. And my supervisor, Jim—good guy, known him for fifteen years—he walked in and saw me. He sat me down, closed the door, and I just spilled it. I told him about the thoughts. I told him how scared I was that I was starting to believe them. And he was the one who told me I needed to come in here. He said, "You can't mess around with that kind of thinking, you gotta talk to somebody." So... no, I haven't made a plan or tried to do anything, but the thoughts... yeah, they're there. And they're exactly why I came in.

My wife made my favorite chicken fried steak the other night and I chewed it like it was cardboard. It's like the part of me that feels good about things just packed up and walked off the job.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this way?\n\nPatient: Well, doc, if I had to put a pin in it... Yeah, doc, every single day. It’s... well, it’s been about two weeks now. Two weeks since she packed up and left Georgia for the military. And I mean every single day since then, it’s just been this... this heavy, dark cloud sitting right on my chest.

And then she hugged me, and she hugged her mom, and she got in and drove off to start basic training. 

And ever since those taillights disappeared down the street... man, it's just been this constant emptiness. Two whole weeks of it. I wake up, and for a split second, I forget she's gone, but then it hits me all over again. And it's not just missing her, you know? It's natural to miss your kid when they leave the nest, I know that. But it's like all the color just drained right out of the world the minute she crossed the state line. Two whole weeks of just... nothing. Just waking up and feeling completely hollowed out, day in and day out, without a single break. I keep thinking maybe tomorrow I'll wake up and feel like my old self, the guy who gets things done, but nope. Every day, same gray emptiness, from the minute I open my eyes till I'm staring at that ceiling fan at night.

It was quiet, gave me something to do with my hands. \n\nAnd on Sundays, man, Sundays used to be my favorite. I’d go to church with the wife, and afterwards, I’d be the guy staying late, standing out in the parking lot or the vestibule, just shooting the breeze with the other guys for an hour. And then I'd come home, get in my recliner, and watch the Falcons game. I never missed a game. Even when they were having a rough season, I’d be right there yelling at the TV. \n\nBut lately... I don't know. I walk past the garden and the weeds are taking over, and I just look at it. I look at the tomatoes rotting on the vine, and I don't even care. I walk into the garage and see my workbench, and it just... it feels like it belongs to somebody else. Like some other guy used to stand there and sand wood. I haven't turned on a football game in weeks. And church... I still go because my wife wants me to, but the minute the service is over, I just make a beeline for the truck. I don't want to talk to anybody. I don't want to stand around. I just want to go home and sit in the quiet. It’s like all the color just got washed out of everything I used to like doing.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling pleasure or enjoyment from anything at all lately?\n\nPatient: Honestly, doc, like I was just saying... it's just nothing. Zero. I know I just went on a whole tear about the tomato plants, and sanding wood at my bench, and watching the Falcons, and staying after church to talk with the guys... but to answer you straight, no. No pleasure from anything at all. \n\nI even try to force it, I really do. I'll sit down in my recliner and think, \"Okay, I'm gonna watch this game and I'm gonna enjoy it,\" but I just stare at the screen and feel completely empty. I look at all that stuff—my tools, my garden, my Sunday routine—and like I said, it really does just feel like it belongs to somebody else. Like I'm a ghost walking around in my own house looking at some other man's life. \n\nI don't get a kick out of a good meal anymore. My wife made my favorite chicken fried steak the other night and I chewed it like it was cardboard. I don't care about a hot cup of coffee in the morning, I don't even crack a smile when one of the guys on the floor tells a joke. It's just this big, heavy blankness all the time. So, no, I can't think of a single thing that brings me any joy right now. It's like the part of me that feels good about things just packed up and walked off the job.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this way?\n\nPatient: Well, doc, if I had to put a pin in it... I've been trying to figure that out myself, tracing it back, you know? Because a man wants to know why his engine's stalling out. And it seems like this whole... this whole change in me, it’s been going on for right about two weeks now. \n\nIt started right exactly when my youngest—my daughter—she packed up and left Georgia. She joined up with the military. Army, actually. She's always been a tough kid, always wanted to do something big with her life, which I'm proud of, I really am. But man, when the day actually came... we drove her down to the processing station, and I hugged her goodbye, and it just hit me like a ton of bricks. I remember driving back home with my wife, and the truck was just so dead quiet. Usually, we'd have the country station on, or we'd be talking about what we needed to pick up from the grocery store, but I just couldn't say a single word. \n\nAnd ever since that day—which was exactly two weeks ago this past Tuesday—it's like somebody just pulled the plug on me. I thought at first I was just sad to see her go, you know how it is. Any father would be. You raise 'em to leave the nest, you want them to go out and make a life, but it still aches when they finally fly. But it didn't get better. Day three, day four, week one, week two... the house just feels huge and empty now, even with the wife there, and this heavy feeling just kept settling in deeper and deeper. So yeah, it’s been two weeks. Two solid weeks since she shipped out that I've been stuck like this.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any thoughts of actually acting on these feelings of not waking up, or of harming yourself in any way?\n\nPatient: Well, doc... that’s... that’s the real reason I’m sitting in this chair right now. Because, see, it started out as just this heavy feeling, like I said, just feeling like everything was gray and empty after my girl left. But then... then it started getting darker. \n\nI’d be lying in bed at night, staring up at the ceiling fan going round and round, and my wife would be asleep next to me, and I’d just think... \"What if I just didn't wake up?\" And at first, it was just a passing thought, you know? Like, \"Man, it would be so much easier to just sleep through all this.\" But then it started sticking. It started playing on a loop in my head. My daughter’s off starting her life, she doesn't need a dad who can't even get out of his recliner.\" \n\nIt got to the point where it wasn't just a thought anymore, it felt like... like this awful, heavy truth that I couldn't shake. I’ve always been the provider, the guy who takes care of things, and suddenly my own brain is telling me the best way to take care of them is to just... not be here. \n\nI didn't tell my wife. I couldn't. But I was at work, sitting in my office at the plant, and I just... I broke down. I don't cry. I'm a 57-year-old manager, I don't sit at my desk and cry. But I did. And my supervisor, Jim—good guy, known him for fifteen years—he walked in and saw me. He sat me down, closed the door, and I just spilled it. I told him about the thoughts. I told him how scared I was that I was starting to believe them. And he was the one who told me I needed to come in here. And they're exactly why I came in.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost any weight recently?\n\nPatient: Well, doc, since you ask... yeah, I suppose I have. I end up wrapping it back up or just throwing it right in the trash before I go back on the floor. \n\nIt's the same thing at home. I don't feel hungry, I don't crave anything, I don't look forward to eating. Thick, heavy mud, right up to my waist. \n\nYou know, I've been managing the floor at the plant for a long time, and usually, I'm the guy pacing up and down, checking the lines, talking to the foremen, always on the move. I just stared at him blankly for what felt like a whole minute before I could spit out a basic answer. It's embarrassing, honestly. \n\nAnd the guys at work, they're definitely noticing. People keep pulling me aside, asking if I'm coming down with something, asking if I'm sick or if I need to go home and sleep off a bug. Because they see it. Completely stuck in the mud.\n\nDoctor: Have you been experiencing these feelings of sadness and emptiness every day since your daughter left?\n\nPatient: Yeah, doc, every single day. We were standing out in the driveway, right there in front of the house we've lived in for twenty years. Well, doc, that's... yeah. That’s a big part of it, actually. And when you say "more than half the days," I gotta be honest, it's every single day. 

My wife was just getting on me about the yard the other day. I usually... well, I used to love messing with my tomato plants. I got this little patch out back, raised beds I built myself a few years ago, and usually by this time of year I'm out there every evening. I don't know, it's like looking at a neighbor's yard. Like it belongs to somebody else entirely. 

Same goes for my workbench out in the garage. I usually spend hours out there just sanding wood, working on little projects, making birdhouses or fixing up old chairs for folks. The smell of the sawdust, the feel of the grain smoothing out under my hands... it used to settle my mind after a long shift at the plant. Now, the tools are just gathering dust. I walk right past the bench and don't even care to flick the light on. 

And it ain't just the chores or the hobbies, either. Sundays... Sundays used to be my favorite day of the week. We'd go to church, and I was always the guy staying after, drinking that terrible percolator coffee in the fellowship hall, just talking everybody's ear off about how their week went. Then I'd come home, settle into my recliner, and watch the Falcons play. I've been a Falcons fan my whole life, through all the heartbreak, you know? But the last couple of Sundays since my girl left? I didn't even care to turn the TV on to check the score. I sat in the pew at church, and the minute the pastor said "amen," I was out the door. I didn't want to talk to a single soul. 

So, yeah. All the stuff that used to make me, well, *me*... I just look at all that lately like it belongs to somebody else. It's like I don't even recognize the guy who used to enjoy those things.

Well, yeah. That’s... I guess that’s a different question, but the answer is still yes. It’s funny you ask it that way, because I was just standing at the kitchen window yesterday—or maybe it was Tuesday, the days are just kind of running together into one long gray stretch right now—and I was looking out at my yard. 

I usually take a lot of pride in my tomato plants. I got these big Beefsteaks I’ve been babying since the spring, you know, tying them up to the stakes, pinching off the suckers, making sure the soil is just right. Usually, I'd be out there every single evening with the hose, just enjoying the quiet and getting my hands dirty. It's peaceful. But now? I look out there and the vines are starting to droop, the bugs are getting to 'em, and I just... I don't care. 

And it ain't just the yard, either. I got a little workbench out in the garage. I like to tinker, do a little woodworking. Nothin' fancy, just sanding down some wood at my bench, making little birdhouses or shelves just to keep my hands busy. The smell of the sawdust, the rhythm of the sandpaper... usually that settles my mind right down after a long week at the plant. But I walked out there the other day to grab a screwdriver, saw my sander and my wood scraps sitting there, and just felt absolutely nothing. It was just a pile of junk to me. The responsibilities are just piling up around me, and I'm just watching it happen. So, yes. Yes, it is interfering. It's interfering with absolutely everything. I just... I look out there and the vines are starting to droop, the bugs are getting to 'em, and I just... I don't care. \n\nAnd it ain't just the yard, either. I got a little workbench out in the garage. The smell of the sawdust, the rhythm of the sandpaper... usually that settles my mind right down after a long week at the plant. Turned right around and went back inside. \n\nSame thing with Sundays. Usually, I'm the first one parked in his recliner to watch the Falcons play, hollering at the screen, getting all worked up over the play-calling. Or at church, you know? I don't want to touch my tools or my plants. \n\nI used to mess with my tomato plants, sand wood at my bench, watch the Falcons, and stay after church talking, but lately... I don't know, doc.
